1 INTRODUCTION
Twenty years on from the first sub-Neptune discoveries (Santos et al.
2004; Rivera et al. 2005), understanding their nature still remains a
mystery (e.g. Bean et al. 2021). With typical sizes between ∼2−4𝑅⊕,
and orbital periods ≲100 days, sub-Neptunes orbit ∼50% of Sun-
like stars (Petigura et al. 2013; Batalha et al. 2013; Fressin et al. 2013).
Sub-Neptunes sit above the “radius valley”, an observed paucity of
planets at ∼1.8𝑅⊕, although its exact location varies with orbital
period and stellar mass (e.g. Fulton et al. 2017; Petigura et al. 2018;
Van Eylen et al. 2018; Petigura et al. 2022; Ho & Van Eylen 2023).
Their counterparts, referred to as super-Earths, sit below the valley.
Crucially, mass measurements have shown that the bulk density for
planets above and below the valley are markedly different (e.g. Wu
& Lithwick 2013; Weiss & Marcy 2014; Rogers 2015; Wolfgang
et al. 2016; Chen & Kipping 2017). Super-Earths are consistent
with a rocky, Earth-like composition. Conversely, sub-Neptunes have
much lower bulk densities, suggesting the presence of low-density
compositional components within these planets. The radius valley
can thus also be interpreted as an approximate delineation between
planet types of different bulk densities (Luque & Pallé 2022). Despite
the discovery of thousands of sub-Neptunes, their compositions and
formation pathways are still highly debated.
Two major hypotheses exist to explain these observations. In the
“gas dwarf” scenario, super-Earths and sub-Neptunes formed from a
single population of progenitor planets with thick primordial H2/He-

disc (e.g. Lee et al. 2014; Ginzburg et al. 2016). Then, through at-

Ginzburg et al. 2016), core-powered mass loss (Ginzburg et al. 2018)
and XUV photoevaporation (Owen & Wu 2013; Lopez & Fortney
2013), planets that are smaller in mass and closer to their host stars
were stripped of their envelopes, leaving behind bare cores. These
rocky cores thus formed the population of super-Earths, whereas
the planets that could retain their H2/He envelopes formed the sub-
Neptune population. This evolutionary model is supported by di-
rect observations of escaping hydrogen and helium (e.g. Dos Santos
2023).
On the other hand, the “water world” hypothesis states that the
radius valley represents the end-product of two distinct planet for-
mation pathways (e.g. Mordasini et al. 2009; Venturini et al. 2016;
Raymond et al. 2018; Zeng et al. 2019; Mousis et al. 2020; Burn et al.
2024a). Rocky super-Earths were formed in the inner regions of pro-
toplanetary discs, where the major solid components are silicates.
Sub-Neptunes formed beyond the water-ice line, where the available
solid mass increases due to the condensation of volatile species. They
accrete large quantities of ice/water content (typically ∼50% of their
mass) and then migrate inwards to the orbital locations we observe
them at today.
Seeking evidence in favour of either model at the population level
is a complex challenge, largely due to the compositional degeneracy
when only measuring a planet’s bulk density (e.g. Rogers 2015; Bean
et al. 2021). Models for both mechanisms can reproduce demographic
observations in various parameter spaces, such as orbital period,

gas dwarfs and water worlds, which relies on the characterisation of
planet demographics at early stellar ages. We exploit the difference in
predicted mean molecular weights in the envelopes of such planets,
which produce very different evolutionary behaviour at young ages.
Gas dwarf envelopes are expected to be H2/He-dominated, yielding

high mean molecular weights and small scale heights. The thick-

2.1 Gas Dwarfs
For our simplest gas dwarf models, we assume a gas mean molecular
weight of 𝜇= 2.35 atomic mass units (amu), appropriate for Solar-
metallicity gas (e.g. Anders & Grevesse 1989), a gas adiabatic index
of 𝛾= 7/5 for molecular hydrogen, and interpolate the Rosseland
mean opacity tables from Kempton et al. (2023) for Solar-metallicity
gas. For the cores of gas dwarfs, multiple studies have shown that
their interiors are consistent with an Earth-like composition (e.g.
Owen & Wu 2017; Gupta & Schlichting 2020; Rogers & Owen
2021; Rogers et al. 2023a). Thus, we assume a core mean molecular
weight of 𝜇c = 60, motivated by Earth (Szurgot 2015). To calculate
the core radius, 𝑅c, we adopt the mass-radius relations of Fortney
et al. (2007), assuming an Earth-like interior composition of 25%
iron, 75% rock, as inferred from Rogers & Owen (2021); Rogers
et al. (2023a).
Hydrogen-dominated gas is susceptible to atmospheric escape,
which can include mechanisms such as boil-off during disc dispersal
(Owen & Wu 2016; Ginzburg et al. 2016; Rogers et al. 2024a), core-
powered mass loss (e.g. Ginzburg et al. 2018; Gupta & Schlichting
2019; Misener et al. 2024) and XUV photoevaporation (e.g. Owen &
Jackson 2012; Kubyshkina & Fossati 2022; Schulik & Booth 2022;
Caldiroli et al. 2022). For simplicity, we choose to model planets af-
ter the protoplanetary disc has fully dissipated. As shown in Rogers
et al. (2024a), boil-off and core-powered mass loss should dominate
during disc dispersal, then photoevaporation dictates the planetary
outflow once the gas disc is optically thin to XUV photons through
its midplane. Nevertheless, photoevaporation and core-powered mass
loss are similar hydrodynamic escape processes (Owen & Schlicht-
ing 2024), and thus, this simplifying assumption has little effect on
our results. We calculate photoevaporative mass loss rates with the

2.2 Water Worlds
For our simplest water world models, we assume a pure steam enve-
lope with a mean molecular weight of 𝜇= 18 amu, a gas adiabatic
index of 𝛾= 4/3, and Rosseland mean opacities from Kempton et al.
(2023) for pure H2O gas. For the core, we assume an interior compo-
sition of 50% rock, 50% water, as predicted by population synthesis
models (e.g. Mordasini et al. 2009; Raymond et al. 2018; Zeng et al.
2019; Venturini et al. 2016; Mousis et al. 2020; Burn et al. 2024a).
This yields a core mean molecular weight of 𝜇c = 27 amu. We use
this composition in the mass-radius relations of Fortney et al. (2007)
to calculate a core radius, 𝑅c. Similar to the steam models of Rogers
et al. (2025), we choose not to consider the atmospheric escape of
steam-dominated (or, more generally, high mean molecular weight)
envelopes due to the many uncertainties of this mechanism. Little
is currently known about how processes such as molecular disso-
ciation/ionisation, drag, diffusion, and line-cooling may affect the
escape of high mean molecular weight envelopes, and thus, we leave
this for future work. Nevertheless, studies have shown that water-rich
sub-Neptunes should store most of their water in their rocky interiors
(Dorn & Lichtenberg 2021; Luo et al. 2024), meaning that we need
only consider small envelope mass fractions, which may either suffer
from inefficient atmospheric escape and/or may be replenished from
their outgassing interiors.

3.1 Gas dwarf vs. water world evolution
We now consider the evolution of gas dwarfs and water worlds. Figure
2 demonstrates their evolution in orange and blue, respectively. We
show planet models with core masses of 4𝑀⊕, 6𝑀⊕and 8𝑀⊕in
solid, dashed and dotted lines, respectively. Models are initialised at
𝑡= 5 Myrs. In the left-hand panel, we construct “minimal” models,
as described in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, which represent the simplest
physical construction of each formation scenario. Under this set of
models, gas dwarfs and water worlds have bulk mean molecular
weights of 𝜇= 2.35 amu and 𝜇= 18.0 amu, respectively, initial
envelope mass fractions of 𝑋= 0.05 and 𝑋= 0.01, respectively, and
orbital periods of 10 days. Gas dwarfs and water worlds converge
in size after ∼1 Gyr due to their internal composition producing
the same radius: water worlds with water-rich, low-density cores and
compact envelopes, gas dwarfs with rocky/iron-rich, high-density
cores and extended envelopes. However, their evolution is divergent
at early ages. The low bulk mean molecular weight of gas dwarf
envelopes means that the energy of formation, which is abundant at
early times, puffs the planet up significantly when compared to water
worlds. This is particularly apparent for planet ages ≲100 Myrs.
In the right-hand panel of Figure 2, we consider more complex
models of gas dwarfs and water worlds, informed by recent theoret-
ical and observational studies. In the case of gas dwarfs, multiple
works have shown that the chemical interaction of Solar-metallicity
gas with a magma ocean at high temperatures will result in an in-
crease in envelope mean molecular weight (Kite & Schaefer 2021;
Schlichting & Young 2022; Misener & Schlichting 2022; Misener
et al. 2023; Rogers et al. 2024b; Young et al. 2024). Most notably,
chemical reactions between hydrogen gas and molten silicate can pro-
duce large quantities of vapour species such as SiO, MgO, FeO and
H2O, increasing the mean molecular weight above Solar values. As
an example, recent JWST observations of TOI-270 d, an archetypal
temperate sub-Neptune, have been interpreted with a mean molecu-
lar weight of 𝜇∼5 amu (Benneke et al. 2024), consistent with the
global chemical equilibrium models of Schlichting & Young (2022);
Rogers et al. (2024b). To capture this effect in our simple evolu-
tionary formalism, we produce gas dwarf models with bulk mean
molecular weights of 𝜇= 5.0 amu, which is indicative of mixed
miscible envelopes. Since H2O is a dominant opacity carrier, we
use the Rosseland mean opacities from Kempton et al. (2023) for a
H2/He/H2O mixture with a H2O mass fraction of 60% to reproduce
this bulk mean molecular weight. We continue to assume atmospheric
escape according to Equation 11 with the same efficiencies as in the
minimal gas dwarf model, but highlight that molecular cooling and
drag should reduce such mass loss rates. This model thus provides
an upper limit in terms of contraction rate as a test of whether the
mixed-envelope models can still be distinguished at early ages. In or-
der for this model to reproduce the typical sizes of sub-Neptunes, we
must increase its envelope mass fraction, as highlighted in Thorngren
& Fortney (2019); Misener & Schlichting (2022). For the right-hand
panel of Figure 2, gas dwarfs have an initial envelope mass fraction

the population-level impacts of bulk mean molecular weight on the
sizes of young sub-Neptunes. Nevertheless, convection inhibition can

4.1 Modelling synthetic transit surveys
The prerequisite for our population models is that they reproduce the
observed exoplanet population at late times ≳1 Gyr. To do so, we
choose to compare the models at late times with the California Ke-
pler Survey (CKS) from Petigura et al. (2022). We seek to construct
underlying models that, when injected through the CKS pipeline, re-
produce the observed (biased) population. For each model, we evolve
106 planets, with stellar masses drawn from a Gaussian distribution
with a mean of 1𝑀⊙and a standard deviation of 0.3𝑀⊙(Rogers
et al. 2021). We also randomly draw a disc dispersal time, which
defines the initial time for each planet model, uniformly drawn be-
tween 3 Myrs and 10 Myrs (e.g. Kenyon & Hartmann 1995; Ercolano
et al. 2011; Koepferl et al. 2013). The typical ages of host stars in
the CKS catalogue are in the range of ≈1 −10 Gyrs (e.g. Berger
et al. 2020). Hence, we terminate each planet model at a random
time, uniformly drawn between these limits. Finally, we statistically
model observational uncertainty in planetary radii by introducing a
random Gaussian perturbation to each planet radius with zero mean
and a standard deviation of 5% the planet’s true size.

We stress that comparing models at early evolutionary times is
only valid if the population models reproduce the observations at
late times. In order to reproduce the CKS sample at ∼1 −10 Gyrs,
both population-level models require different planetary initial con-
ditions, including initial envelope mass fraction distributions, core
mass distributions, and orbital period distributions. We discuss these
in the following sections.
4.2 Gas dwarf population model
For the gas dwarf case, both super-Earths and sub-Neptunes are
drawn from the same underlying population, and atmospheric es-
cape is responsible for separating the two sub-populations over time
and forming the radius valley. We use the inferred underlying dis-
tributions from Rogers & Owen (2021), who fitted the XUV pho-
toevaporation “minimal” model from Section 2.1 to the CKS data
of Fulton & Petigura (2018) using a Bayesian hierarchical model.
Both the core mass and initial envelope mass fraction distributions
are parameterised using Bernstein polynomials of 5th order. These
